div.p: BACKGROUND Collision tumors, defined as the coexistence of two distinct neoplasms with independent origins in the same anatomical location, are rare entities that pose diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. While pituitary adenomas and meningiomas are individually common intracranial tumors, their coexistence as collision tumors is exceptionally uncommon, with only a handful of cases reported in the literature. Even fewer involve growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenomas, and none have involved sphenoid wing meningiomas to date.

div.head: OBSERVATIONS
div.p: The authors present the case of a 54-year-old female who presented with progressive expressive aphasia, right-sided weakness, gait imbalance, and memory decline. Initial MRI demonstrated a large dural-based mass involving the left sphenoid wing and sellar region; the tumor was resected in staged procedures and diagnosed as a meningothelial meningioma. Fourteen months later, follow-up imaging revealed a distinct sellar lesion. Endoscopic endonasal resection demonstrated a pituitary adenoma extensively involved by the meningioma, establishing the diagnosis of a collision tumor.

div.head: LESSONS
div.p: The authors highlight the importance of recognizing the potential for dual pathology in complex intracranial tumors. This case describes the limitations of preoperative imaging in diagnosing collision tumors. Careful long-term surveillance and multidisciplinary management are essential for accurate diagnosis and optimal treatment of collision tumors.

Collision tumors represent a rare category of neoplasms wherein two or more distinct tumors grow in spatial proximity within the human body. 1 The exact pathogenesis of intracranial collision tumors remains unclear.Collision tumors should be distinguished from mixed tumors, which consist of two distinct neoplasms with histologically admixed cell types. 2 These rare entities represent a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge due to unusual imaging findings, challenging resection, and divergent histopathology, which leads to difficult treatment decisions in the molecular era. 1 While meningiomas and pituitary adenomas are individually common and well-documented tumors, a collision tumor of these two neoplasm types is exceptionally rare, with only 10 cases described in the literature to date. 3 Of those previously documented cases, only 3 reported growth hormone (GH)-secreting pituitary adenoma, none of which described collision with a sphenoid wing meningioma. Indeed, the only meningioma collisions reported in the literature are sella based or had an unspecified location. Here, we present a surgical case report to describe a rare example of a collision tumor between a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma and sphenoid wing meningioma.

div.head: Illustrative Case
div.p: A 54-year-old female with a history of diabetes mellitus (DM) type 2 presented with expressive aphasia, ataxia related to right-sided weakness, and progressively worsening short-term memory loss over 7-8 months. Physical examination was notable for unstable, narrowbased gait and no other neurological deficits. MRI revealed a 4. left petroclival region extending to the middle cranial fossa, cavernous sinus, sellar/suprasellar region, left tentorial leaflet, and posterior clivus with indentation of the left pons (Fig. 1A-C). There was complete encasement of the left internal carotid artery, left posterior communicating artery, and left posterior cerebral artery with abutment of the basilar artery and mass effect on the optic chiasm.

The decision was made to proceed with debulking of the left sphenoid wing and middle cranial fossa lesion through a modified orbitozygomatic approach, followed by a left retrosigmoid craniectomy 6 months later for resection of the petroclival extension into the prepontine cistern and exerting mass effect on the brainstem (Fig. 1D-I). Preoperative pituitary function tests were not drawn prior to surgery.

She recovered well after these surgeries, with improving V2 and V3 distribution numbness, left oculomotor palsy, left eye vision, diplopia, and left eye ptosis. She continued to have DM controlled with metformin.

Histopathological analysis from the modified orbitozygomatic craniotomy demonstrated a moderately cellular meningothelial neoplasm forming large syncytial lobules and occasional vague whorls with frequent intervening fibrocollagenous septae and scattered lymphocytes. No brain invasion was seen, and mitoses were rare. CD45
was positive in the lymphocytic tissue, the Ki-67 index was 2%, and SSTR2 showed strong and diffuse staining supportive of meningothelial meningioma, CNS WHO grade 1.

Given the anatomical proximity of the lesion to the pituitary gland, pituitary function tests were ordered 4 months after the patient's second surgery. At the 8-month follow-up, her insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) and GH levels were paradoxically elevated at 601 ng/mL and 56.8 ng/mL, respectively. Although the patient had uncontrolled type 2 DM in the setting of a healthy diet and body mass index, and had always had large, coarse hands, at this time, she reported that her hands had been growing and that her rings had become tight, suggestive of progressive acromegaly. MRI was performed and demonstrated a T2 hypointense, hypoenhancing component at the right side of the sella concerning for a concurrent functional somatotroph adenoma (Fig. 1G-I).

The patient underwent an endoscopic endonasal approach for pituitary mass resection 1.5 years after the second stage of mass resection. Intraoperatively, it was observed that the sellar/suprasellar tumor was embedded within the meningioma with extension toward the right cavernous sinus. The anterior inferior and right lateral aspects of the tumor were debulked (Fig. 1J-L). Histopathological analysis demonstrated a structure consistent with pituitary adenoma with positivity for GH and negativity for the other pituitary hormone markers, consistent with a sparsely granulated somatotroph adenoma. There was also a separate specimen consistent with her previously diagnosed CNS WHO grade 1 meningothelial meningioma (Fig. 2). The patient's postoperative course was unremarkable, and she was discharged on postoperative day 3 without signs of CSF leakage.

div.head: FIG. 1. A-C:
div.p: At the last follow-up, 14 months after resection of her pituitary adenoma via the endoscopic endonasal approach, the patient's diplopia and facial numbness continued to improve. Her IGF-1 and GH levels have trended downwards (448 ng/mL and 5.2 ng/mL, respectively) postoperatively but are still elevated, and her symptoms of acromegaly are stable. A timeline of the events for this case is shown in Fig. 3.

div.head: Observations
div.p: We present a unique case of a collision tumor involving a petroclival/sphenoid wing meningioma and functional somatotroph adenoma. This report highlights a rare pathology and highlights the need for early recognition in order to treat both pathologies appropriately. This case is unique not only because of the anatomical location of the meningioma and the surgical objective to alleviate mass effect, but also for the subsequent discovery of paradoxically elevated IGF-1 when evaluating for postoperative compressive hypopituitarism as the meningioma grew into the sella. This unique case of a sphenoid wing meningioma involved by a pituitary adenoma highlights the complex intricacies of diagnosis, surgical approach, and postoperative management in patients with collision tumors.

Pituitary adenomas represent a diverse group of tumors of the pituitary gland and are a common neoplasm type, with previous studies describing an estimated prevalence of 16.7%, present in up to 14.4% of autopsy studies and 22.5% of radiography studies. 4 Meningiomas are also common, representing approximately 53.1% of benign CNS tumors. 5 Both neoplasms are more common in females and adults. 3,6 However, a collision tumor involving the coexistence of meningioma and pituitary adenoma in the sella is extremely rare.

In a recent review of the literature, Baldawa and Raikhailkar identified 11 cases, including their own, of a collision tumor involving pituitary adenomas and meningiomas in the sella. 3 These 11 cases represent all previously published examples of this rare pathological phenomenon. However, only 3 of the cases in this study involved a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma; most pituitary adenomas in these collision tumors were nonfunctioning, and one involved a Cushing adenoma. Additionally, all prior reports presented initially with acromegaly; the presence of a meningioma was detected in 1 case based on preoperative MRI findings showing differential enhancement between the intrasellar and parasellar/retrosellar lesions, 7 and in the other 2 cases it was diagnosed after a craniotomy was performed for parasellar residual following an initial endoscopic endonasal resection. 2 In our case, the patient presented with weakness and aphasia due to marked mass effect from a substantial sphenoid wing meningioma causing entrapment and dilatation of the left lateral ventricle (Fig. 1), and it was not until after a two-staged open debulking of this lesion that symptoms of acromegaly developed, leading to the diagnosis and treatment of the pituitary adenoma. It is unclear why the patient did not have progressive acromegaly at initial presentation. One possible explanation is that her weakness and aphasia were more obvious symptoms, causing the more subtle features of acromegaly to go unnoticed. Another explanation is that compression of the pituitary adenoma by the meningioma may lead to inhibition of GH secretion, such that decompressing the adenoma led to increased GH secretion and development of symptoms. Our case provides the most recent example of this rare collision tumor involving a functional somatotroph pituitary adenoma and a meningioma, further contributing to the understanding of the coexistence of these two neoplasm types in the skull base.

Diagnosis of a collision tumor in the sella presents unique challenges. Because of their similar radiological signatures, MRI alone is insufficient for differentiating pituitary adenoma and meningioma, let alone diagnosing a collision tumor involving the two types. 2 Histological examination and confirmation is required. Sellar meningiomas and pituitary adenomas are frequently confused for each other. 8 In a review of 57 cases involving pituitary adenomas and sellar meningiomas, Kwancharoen et al. found that 11% of the cases were erroneously diagnosed as the other. 9 In our case, the tumor was initially characterized as a petroclival/sphenoid wing meningioma extending into the sellar region. The delayed clinical manifestation of acromegaly is a distinctive feature of our case, raising important considerations for endocrine and postoperative management. Our case is also unique in the management of the collision tumor. Whereas previously documented cases of collision tumors opted for the endonasal transsphenoidal approach with or without additional craniotomies, 2,3,10,11 given the initial diagnosis of a sphenoid wing meningioma invading the sellar region, we performed an initial retrosigmoid approach, followed by an endoscopic endonasal approach for the GH-secreting pituitary adenoma.

This case highlights the importance of a thorough preoperative endocrinologic workup for tumors involving the sellar or parasellar FIG. 2. Representative H&E pathology slide showing features consistent with a WHO grade 1 meningioma (right) and pituitary adenoma (left) as well as the interface between the two distinct tumor subtypes. Original magnification ×200. regions. Had pituitary function tests been obtained before the first surgery, the diagnosis of two distinct tumor entities would have been made sooner. However, the initial surgical approach would not have changed, as our decision was guided by the acute presentation of the patient. The modified orbitozygomatic craniotomy was indicated to debulk the anterior and middle fossa disease burden to relieve the symptomatic obstructive hydrocephalus and entrapment of the left lateral ventricle. This was followed by a retrosigmoid craniotomy to address the residual mass effect on the brainstem. Focused on improving symptomatic mass effect, we were initially less concerned with the sellar disease. The key learning point is that in complex skull base lesions, surgical decision-making must involve patient-specific decisions and a thorough preoperative diagnostic workup, and clinicians should maintain suspicion for dual pathology when there is involvement of the sella, even in the presence of an extra-axial tumor.

For sellar lesions, the first diagnosis considered is typically pituitary adenoma. Zhao et al., the authors of the previously mentioned study that published 3 cases that serve as the first examples of a collision tumor between GH-secreting pituitary adenoma and meningioma, found no other instances of GH-secreting pituitary adenoma and meningioma coexisting in their literature review. 2 Rather, collision tumors involving pituitary adenoma more frequently included other types of neoplasms such as Rathke's cleft cysts, 12 lymphomas, 13 other adenomas, [14][15][16] craniopharyngiomas, 2,17 and gangliocytomas. 14,[18][19][20] The exact pathogenesis of intracranial collision tumors remains unclear; several hypotheses have been proposed, with some researchers suggesting that the microenvironment of one tumor influences the growth of the other. 18,20,21 The origin and coexistence of sellar meningiomas and pituitary adenomas remain poorly understood. Previous studies have suggested a relationship between GH-secreting pituitary tumors and the development of intracranial meningioma. 21 In our case of GH-secreting adenoma involved by meningioma, one hypothesis postulated is that GH from the GH-secreting adenoma induces the growth of the meningioma (although in our case, features of acromegaly were not evident until after the meningioma was debulked). There is some evidence that corroborates this hypothesis. While there are no overlapping genetic factors between pituitary adenomas and meningiomas as of now, 22,23 75% of meningiomas express receptors for GH. 24 While GH-secreting adenomas make up 9%-11% of all pituitary adenomas, 25 De Vries et al. found that a higher proportion (30.6%) of pituitary adenomas with concomitant meningioma were GH-secreting. 10 GH-producing pituitary adenomas are the most common functional adenomas found coexisting with meningioma. 22 A second hypothesis for the explanation of this type of collision tumor is the association between radiation therapy of pituitary adenoma and the development of post-radiation therapy meningioma. Several cases and reviews have documented the formation of meningioma as a long-term effect of radiotherapy for pituitary adenoma. [26][27][28] However, in our case, no radiotherapy was administered for either the pituitary adenoma or the meningioma, ruling out radiation as a contributing factor.

div.head: Lessons
div.p: We describe the diagnosis and treatment of a collision tumor with a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma involved by a meningothelial meningioma. The tumor was initially thought to be a larger meningioma occupying the sphenoid wing, tuberculum sellae, and sella, but later was recharacterized as a somatotroph adenoma with accompanying acromegaly, underscoring the diagnostic challenges associated with collision tumors and complex dual tumor pathology in the skull base region. Importantly, preoperative pituitary function testing was not obtained in this case. However, this omission highlights a critical consideration: a lesion involving the sella or parasellar region warrants a thorough preoperative endocrine evaluation, even when radiographic features are suggestive of a meningioma, as such testing may facilitate earlier recognition of concurrent pituitary pathology. This case delineates the limitations of preoperative imaging in diagnosing collision tumors and emphasizes the necessity of long-term follow-up and histological examination for accurate diagnosis. Successful management of this rare phenomenon requires a multidisciplinary approach between neuro-oncologists, neuropathologists, and neurosurgeons.
